# Copper January 2012 

- The start of a new year evidently brought with it fresh optimism as copper prices rallied through the month and broke through what over the past few months had become a resistance level of c.$8000/t.  The opportunity to take a fresh look at the fundamentals was perhaps behind a consensus forming that even under a sluggish demand scenario, despite the implied growth in supply (on paper at least), achieving this will not be without its challenges and in any event 2012 does appear to be shaping up to be another year of tightness in the copper market. 

- There is a cautious tone to the start of the year of the dragon, while market participants will be hoping that the disasters that are typically associated with this Chinese year are not economic in nature.  As with 2011, global demand growth will come from China, with prospects in Europe and the US at best described as muted.  We forecast global demand growth of 3.4% this year before rising to 4.4% in 2013. 

- Thus far in this year’s Mating Season, no single set of terms has been universally adopted.  It may be that this year’s long-term market ends up being segregated into regional benchmarks.  For example, recent deals in China appear to be aligned with Anglo’s terms ($60.5/t & 6.05c/lb) while Europe and Japan may be successful in maintaining Freeport’s reference numbers of $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb.  Clearly it is still too early to establish (what, in any event, is unlikely to be) a definitive benchmark for 2012, given the sheer number of outstanding deals still to be concluded.  If subsequent settlements in Europe and Japan were to deviate from those fixed thus far, then the concept of a regional benchmark would not be applicable and some mechanism to calculate a representative global average would need to be established.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**New year brings new hope** The start of a new year evidently brought with it fresh optimism as copper prices rallied through the month and broke through what over the past few months had become a resistance level of c.$8000/t.  The opportunity to take a fresh look at the fundamentals was perhaps behind a consensus for

ming that even under a sluggish demand scenario, despite the implied growth in supply (on paper at least), achieving this will not be without its challenges and in any event 2012 does appear to be shaping up to be another year of tightness in the copper market. 

**Focus on China as we enter the dragon** The month as a whole has been good for copper bulls, although when looking back to the start of January, the first week of the year gave no real indication of the rally that was to come.  In fact, despite a gain on the first trading day of the year, cash quotes ebbed lower through the remainder of the first week and it wasn’t until the following week that the rally began in earnest.  It was news that China’s December imports of refined copper hit an all time high that prompted much of the rally on the 10<sup>th</sup> January, although as we note elsewhere in this publication, the strength of those imports were not a reflection robust Chinese demand at the end of the year, just as sluggish imports at the start of 2011 did not reflect weakness then.  The focus remained on China later that week as a further slowdown in inflation there boosted hopes that authorities would have more scope to relax credit in a bid to prevent a hard landing and indeed to encourage additional demand.  Prices shrugged off a downgrade to what felt like half of Europe and the ramping up of Grasberg following the resolution to a strike at this large Indonesian mine and instead focussed on the continued downward trajectory of stocks. 

**Stocks provide fundamental support** Stocks have been falling for a few months now but the rate of decline picked up in pace from the second week of January, while at the same time, cancelled warrants also began to rise appreciably, pointing to further draw downs to come.  Up to the 27th total stocks stood at 333,125 tonnes, a decline of 38,450 tonnes from the end of December, while cancelled warrants rose from 43,425 tonnes at the end of the prior month to 95,825. With much of the material that was held in Asian warehouses already shipped to China following their year end import boom, the reductions then began to come from other regions, with stocks in US locations declining the most through January.  Moreover, the sharp rise in cancelled warrants in the US pointed to further physical withdrawals.  This begged the question of where the material was destined and why.  Although US demand isn’t too bad right now and the general sentiment among US rod makers is of quiet confidence about 2012, this in itself is unlikely to have been the reason for the 17kt stock decline and a 50kt plus increase in cancelled warrants since the end of December.  If US demand isn’t sufficient to pull this level of material out of warehouses, then was it demand elsewhere?  With such a sharp run up in Chinese imports at the end of the year, at least part of this material found its way into increased inventories at semis producers in that country and as such, we expect

a slowdown in the rate of cathode shipments into China in the first quarter. This view is further supported by the fact that the arbitrage window is presently closed and premia have eased back since the end of last year and as such, it does not seem rational to explain these US withdrawals as resulting from strong Chinese demand. In which case, warehouse wars could have been behind the move, with material simply moving out of the system only to go back in, as happened in the US with zinc a few months ago. As it turns out, we understand that the reason behind the increase in US cancelled warrants, at New Orleans in particular, was that a trader was left short of material following the fires at Pan Pacific’s Saganoseki smelter in Japan and at PASAR in the Philippines. That it turns out the material is needed to meet orders is promising for the year ahead from a demand perspective, that it ultimately stemmed from a disruption is less positive for hopes of a more up tempo year for the supply side of the market. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

**Chinese imports finish on a (record) high** As we noted above, imports into China ended the year with a bang, hitting an all time high with full year shipments only modestly down on the preceding year. December’s 78% year-on-year surge to 406.9kt meant that 2011’s total of 2.84Mt was only 3% down on 2010, an impressive outturn given that first half imports were down by almost a third on the prior year. However, it is important to note that the recent increase in imports does not reflect robust demand conditions in the Chinese market, which slowed in the final quarter of the year. Rather, part of the rise stemmed from consumers using up their foreign currency credits before the end of the year and taking advantage of previously lower prices to stock up. The balance was split between copper shipped in for financing purposes and

traders simply turning a profit by arbitraging LME/SHFE price differentials. The breakdown of these three elements is open to debate, although it is hard to argue but that the overall stock that is available to the market has increased and as such, the usual pattern of a first quarter re-stock has at least partly already taken place. This suggests from a fundamental perspective that the pace of imports into China ought to slow in the first quarter of this year. **Premia either up, down or stable** With much of China on holiday during the second half of January it was no surprise that premia edged lower to around the $100/t mark. In Europe, however, trade picked up a little, with premia climbing back up to the $40-60/t level compared to the lowly $25-35/t seen at the end of December and suggestive of a mild pick up in activity following the year end destock. Meanwhile in the US, premia seem to be quoted in a wide range, although 5.0-5.5c/lb seems to be where most of the trade is taking place, amid reasonable demand conditions. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai US c/lb 10

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2012 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Chinese broad shoulders to support global demand growth** From an economic perspective, sentiment across key global markets is not that much different from where it had been for much of last year, with a feeling of malaise casting a dark pall over demand prospects. Nowhere is this more acutely felt than in Europe, where the ongoing failure to resolve the regional debt crisis continues to dampen consumer confidence. The difference this year, however, is that demand weakness is likely to be felt in the first half of the year, while in 2011 it was first quarter strength that prevented a sharper downturn in full year demand in western Europe in particular. As with last year, it will be growth in that key market, China that will drive our global forecast, with a further 8% expansion expected in 2012, although this growth will be weighted towards the second half of the year. We now estimate that global demand growth last year was just under 3% and we now forecast a 3.4% expansion in 2012, the latter being equivalent to some 675kt of metal with over 92% of this increase relating to China. The downside risks across key markets are plain to see, so we will not elaborate here, although it is worth noting that 2011 data is not finalised and as such, 2012 growth could well yet come from a lower starting point. **Risks to supply remain evident** The situation at Grasberg during the final quarter of last year served as a reminder that industrial a

ction remains a significant threat to supply continuity and, as we noted last month, just under 2Mt of production is potentially at risk from labour disputes in 2012. It is also worth mentioning the significant impact of low ore grades on copper output of late that have affected mines such as Bingham Canyon, Escondida, Grasberg and Highland Valley Copper. Improved yields at most of these operations will not occur until the second half of this year and there are other mines that expect to encounter declining head grades in 2012 such as Batu Hijau, Candelaria, Cerro Verde, Norilsk, Phu Kham etc. **2012 to remain fundamentally tight** Our latest refined output and demand growth estimates for 2011 indicate a market deficit of -136kt, which is less severe than previously expected, with this largely being a result of softer demand growth last year. We have also slightly tempered our projection of demand growth for 2012 and this has had the effect of reducing our forecast deficit for this year also. This now stands at -117kt but importantly, this will represent a third year of global deficit and will result in a further reduction in stocks, measured in days of consumption, moving lower to 49 days from 53 in 2011. This will serve to keep copper prices well supported from a fundamental perspective and we forecast an average $8700/t for this year, with cash quotes set to peak in the second quarter in tandem with the usual seasonal upturn in demand. A general improvement in economic activity in 2013 will see demand building on positive momentum, although an expected 4.4% increase in consumption will be easily outmuscled by our forecast 7.6% growth in refined production, even after applying our 5% mine supply disruption. This expansion in output is shaping up to provide a surplus of over half a million tonnes and leads us to project that prices will ebb lower, to $8150/t on average. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

## Consumption 

There is a cautious tone to the start of the year of the dragon, while market participants will be hoping that the disasters that are typically associated with this Chinese year are not economic in nature.  As with 2011, global demand growth will come from China, with prospects in Europe and the US at best described as muted.  We forecast global demand growth of 3.4% this year before rising to 4.4% in 2013. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**North-South divide in European economies** It is fair to say that economic activity across the region slowed into the year end, but this one size fits all approach to assessing the European economy does not adequately describe industrial activity.  For instance, IP fell by 2.6% year on year in November in the euro area, and incidentally the first contraction in over two years, while output in Germany actually increased by 3.6% year on year.  However, in both Italy and Spain, IP has been falling on the prior year for most of the second half of this year.  Despite the slowdown that we know about and that economic data is now affirming, at least some sentiment indicators are looking up, with the key German Ifo indicator rising in January.  This is positive for broader European demand in particular as Germany dwarfs the rest of Europe in terms of its own consumption of copper and indeed, many other metals.  Despite this, Germany’s shoulders will not be broad enough to offset weakness elsewhere, and we forecast a contraction in European demand in 2012. 

**2011 European estimate nudged lower** Our estimate of European demand growth in 2011 has been nudged lower yet again, and with final trade and production data still not available, there could be worse still to come.  We now estimate that European consumption increased by 2.6% to 3.96Mt in 2011, although without the increase in Russian apparent demand, there would have been a contraction in demand. 

**Tariffs drive increase in Russian demand** The increase in Russia was largely as a result of changes to export tariffs at the start of 2011, which resulted in cathode being first processed into wire rod before being exported.  The result was that domestic consumption soared, even if this was more than a little misleading.  Latest results from Russian producers confirm this, with wire rod output at KMEZ, which is owned by the Russian Copper Company, up by 57% in 2011 to 99kt. This increase is broadly in line with our estimate of growth in consumption of refined copper in Russia of 60%. 

**Aurubis calendar Q3 results underline European weakness** The release of Aurubis’ full year results make interesting reading and are perhaps indicative of an earlier slowdown in demand than previously thought.  Wire rod output in the third calendar quart

er fell by 8.5% year on year to 172kt, while output of shapes fell by an even sharper 22% year on year to 42kt. #### **Aurubis Q3 wire rod production – (kt)** 120 240

**Europe cancels doom and gloom** The sharp rise in cancelled warrants and decline in LME inventories have caught attention elsewhere in this publication but it is worth mentioning that inventories have ebbed lower in Europe also. Moreover, cancelled warrants have increased, pointing to further drawdowns from warehouses, which begs the question of where this material going. It is clear that demand is pretty sluggish at the moment but it is also apparent that there was a good deal of de-stocking at producers and consumers at the year end. So, the drawdown could be a reflection of firms needing material to fulfil orders and thus, a very modest re-stock or at least suggesting some activity at semis Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2012 Page 5 of 21 Copper Monthly Update producers. An alternative explanation is that the material is being shipped to China in line with strong demand for imports, if not strong underlying demand. We understand that excess cathode production was being shipped to China by European producers at the end of last year because of the attractiveness of Chinese premia relative to Europe. With European premia back up to the $40-60/t range, and China’s slipping a little, this is perhaps unlikely, especially given that the arbitrage window is presently closed and that we are expecting a slowdown in Chinese imports. **Contraction forecast for 2012** Much of the economic backdrop is pretty gloomy and although we do forecast a decline in European demand this year, things could look a lot worse. Flat demand in key market Germany prevents a more severe contraction across the region as a whole and as such, we expect European consumption to decline by a relatively modest c.1%, with the second half of the year looking much better than the first. ### **Americas** **Rod output in holding pattern in 2011, expect better in 2012** Operating rate run-downs and, in one instance at least, outright shut-down, at US copper rod mills during December pushed national rod output to its lowest level in two years at 89kt vs. 95kt in November, and ensured that full-year rod production of 1.253Mt remained marginally down on the prior year’s 1.262Mt. Rod plants were keen to run down inventory by the year’s end, but still wound up holding more rod (28kt) than both the prior month (24.2kt) and in December 2010 (24.8kt), according to data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS). Still, our conversati

ons with operators reveal a good deal of confidence going into the new year, with expectations of a 5% year-on-year gain in rod output volumes being noted. We have a more cautious 3% improvement plugged into our forecasts for this year, and note also that one player absent from the market last year (Sherburne Metals) should have worked through its re-commissioning phase during Q4 and could add up to 30kt of oxygen-free rod to the market this year. Rod shipments at the national level were down similarly to production at 1.249Mt vs. 1.258Mt. But the domestics also had to contend with a surge in Russian rod imports during 2011 (27.7kt through to November, vs. zero in 2010), and a 7.6% hike in imports from Canada (to 94.9kt for the 11-month period). Behind some of the optimism in rod producers for this year will be a stable construction sector (stable being seen as an improvement on the outright declines of recent years) and continued strength in the automotive sector. Sales of new cars will be driven by a more widespread need for replacement, and could top 14M units this year, according to a leading retailer, or at least approach that level, according to JD Power & Associates’ forecast of 13.8M units. National sales of 12.78M units rose by 10% on 2010’s 11.59M units, according to industry reporter, Automotive News, with Chrysler Group sales up by 26%, Ford Motor Co up by 9% and GMC up by 13%. #### **US copper wire rod production and shipments – (kt)** 150

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2012 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **China** **Apparently demand was quite good last year** The past year has been interesting for watchers of Chinese demand with imports disappointing in the first half of the year and this leading to concerns about the state of domestic consumption. What many in the market failed to grasp, however, was the scale of de-stocking that was taking place in China, and looking at apparent consumption calculations in isolation were failing to fully account for underlying demand. However, with such a sharp run-up in imports in the final part of this year, it is fair to say that looking at apparent demand alone would be overstating true consumption. **Q1 stock build came early** There is typically a build up of stocks at the start of the year as semis producers build up inventory once they have their new annual budget. Producers then tend to work down these stocks through the course of the year. However, given that there was such a sharp rise in imports in the final part of 2011 it is clear that there has been at least some build up of inventory at semis producers. Refined copper imports surged to their highest ever total in December, soa

ring 78% year on year to 406.9kt to finish the year at 2.835Mt, down 3% on 2010’s figure. The sharp rise in imports can be attributed to a number of factors, not least that the absolute price of copper was relatively low in the preceding months but also because of favourable arbitrage. That the arbitrage window was open also meant that material was not clogging up in bonded warehouses. However, that does not mean that this was a reflection of strong demand, rather, there was a combination of re-stocking at semis producers and using copper as a financing vehicle. This re-stock at the end of the year goes a long way to explaining why we expect imports to slow in the first quarter as firms do not need to re-stock to the same degree as usual. However, it is worth noting that imports were relatively weak in the first quarter of 2011 and we are saying that year-on-year comparisons may look good but this will still represent a decline on the fourth quarter of last year. **Semis plants close for holidays** It goes without saying that semis output is likely to have dipped lower during January as producers closed for the Chinese New Year, with many reportedly closing their doors as early as the middle of the month. There should also be no surprise that we expect activity to pick up in February as firms re-start production. The big question of course is where demand will come from in 2012 given broad market expectations of a sluggish construction market and sharply slowing white goods sales. **Demand digging out of a hole** Starting with construction, we believe that 2012 should be a reasonable year for demand for copper, even if new building slows. There was a good deal of activity in the second half of last year in particular as builders rushed to meet targets for the commencement of social housing projects. Anecdotal evidence suggests that some firms simply dug holes in the ground to be able to say that they had started construction, which suggests that much of the work from starts last year will feed through into 2012. In any case, copper consumption typically comes at the end of construction activity and as such, a spurt of housing starts in the second half of last year is actually positive for demand this year. This is why we are relatively sanguine on prospects for sectoral demand. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

**Consumer sectors to enter deep freeze** With the government announcing an end to subsidies for electrical appliances at the end of 2011, in addition to expectations of sluggish exports, the near term outlook for the consumer and ACR sectors looks uncertain. Without doubt, we anticipate a slowd

own in ACR output in particular in 2012 following the breakneck pace of last year, which saw air conditioner production rise by a stunning 26% to 146 million units. Meanwhile, white goods also enjoyed a sharp rise in output, with production of washing machines and refrigerators up by Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2012 Page 7 of 21 Copper Monthly Update an impressive 7.6% and 14% respectively. We do hear rumours of new incentive schemes being introduced although there are no firm details as yet. As we note above, without anything to artificially lift demand from the government, demand from these sectors looks set for a sluggish year in 2012. Other key sectors are more bullish however, and we expect infrastructure spending to maintain solid growth, with this driving investment in the power sector. The build-out of energy networks throughout the western regions in particular remains far from complete and this will support demand this year. Meanwhile, we expect an upturn in demand from the automotive sector in 2012 as sales and production recover from the hangover of purchase incentive schemes coming to and end in 2010. For the year as a whole, we forecast another year of robust demand growth in China, and are looking for a further 8% expansion in refined copper consumption before an easing back in 2013. #### **Production and shipments of copper wire rod and copper semis – (kt)** ||**2009**|**2010**|**2011**|**2011**||||||||| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |||||**Q1**|**Q2**|**Q3**|**Q4**|**Sep**|**Oct**|**Nov**|**Dec**|**Ytd**| |**USA: Production**||||||||||||| |Cu Wire Rod|1071|1262|1253|325|328|311|289|106|105|95|89|1253| |Y-Y % change|-27.9|9.7|-0.7|0.5|2.7|-6.3|0.5|-2.6|-0.3|2.4|-0.6|-0.7| |**USA: Shipments**||||||||||||| |Cu and Cu Alloy Prods|869|980|-|259|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|429| |Y-Y % change|-26.0|12.8|-|7.2|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|5.0| |**Japan: Shipments**||||||||||||| |Cu Wire and Cable|649|681|681|171|163|168|179|59|60|60|58|681| |Y-Y% change|-20.5|5.0|-0.1|1.1|0.0|-3.0|1.7|-2.2|2.6|-0.4|2.9|-0.1| |**Japan: Production**

On a more positive note, however, industrial orders improved sha

rply in November both on a year-on-year and month-onmonth basis, although given the lumpy nature of this series, the IP data is perhaps more indicative of the overall economic environment.  That said, we still expect an upturn in industrial output overall in 2012, with a 5-6% expansion forecast, although clearly, Q2 2010 weakness flatters this growth rate somewhat. 

**Semis shipments in full year slip** Semis shipments were somewhat mixed for the year as a whole with the wire and cable sector doing reasonably well in the circumstances but brass mill shipments weighing on overall growth.  Indeed, wire and cable shipments enjoyed a solid finish to the year, rising 2.9% year on year in December at 58.4kt, and as a result, full year shipments were flat on the prior year at 680.6kt.  However, the performance of brass mill shipments was much worse and they ended with a whimper, sliding at a double-digit rate to leave annual shipments down by 4.8% to 825.1kt. 

**2012 to see c.2% expansion in demand** A weaker than expected decline in activity in the final months of the year have led us to slightly reduce our estimate of demand in Japan last year.  We now estimate that consumption contracted by 3.2% in 2011 at 1.026Mt, while we have also clipped our 2012 forecast a little.  We remain committed to the view that transport and construction will enjoy a modest recovery but the electrical sector will drag and prevent a more robust recovery.  As such, we now expect demand to expand by c.2% this year.

**Automotive to drive recovery in 2012** After a collapse in the aftermath of the earthquake of March 2011, motor vehicle production recovered through the year, with sectoral demand mirroring improvements.  The current year will bring with it some unusually large growth rates in shipments and production through the second quarter of the year in particular, although these are largely a result of base effects from the disruption to output stemming from the disaster that we mentioned above.  For the year as a whole we expect an expansion in production, with domestic demand in particular driving this recovery after domestic sales stagnated in 2011 in a hangover from 2010’s incentive programmes. 

**(Re)construction will also support growth** Demand from the construction sector actually performed quite well last year, with the building of temporary homes supporting semis shipments to the sector.  However, this year we expect the construction of more permanent structures to lift consumption. **More settlements reported in the concentrate Mating Season** Last month we reported that Freeport had concluded long-term contract negotiations with all of its customers and had fixed terms at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb across the board.  We also noted that other sellers had established differing terms to these in China and India.  Escondida concluded deals at $60/t & 6c/lb but with 10% tonnage reductions in H2 2012 while Codelco also finalised its contracts in these countries at the same level but with no tonnage adjustments.

Anglo Chile was also successful in fixing terms in China and India at $60.5/t & 6.05c/lb and, more recently is rumoured to have made a similar deal in another Asian country.  Subsequently, Vale concluded terms with its Chinese partners at $60.5/t & 6.05c/lb as did Antofagasta with respect to its Esperanza contracts.  For Los Pelambres, however, the Chilean miner was able to achieve a high grade premium of $3.5/t & 0.5c/lb, thereby establishing a fifth set of terms ($57/t & 6c/lb) in China for the 2012 Mating Season.  Japan has proven to be a tougher nut to crack with smelters in that country exceedingly reluctant to entertain terms other than those established with Freeport ($63.5/t & 6.35c/lb).  Indeed, it has been rumoured that negotiations between the three major Japanese buyers and Escondida have now ended with no deals having been struck given the seller’s insistence on maintaining the same terms as were achieved in China and India.  Meanwhile, European smelting companies are also holding their ground on keeping with the Freeport numbers with at least six deals (three for Aurubis, two for Atlantic and one for New Boliden) concluded at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb. 

**No benchmark as yet** Although the absolute difference in these various Mating Season settlements may not be substantial, this does create problems for those contracts that reference a benchmark as, thus far, there are no single sets of terms that have been universally adopted.  It may be that this year’s long-term market ends up being segregated into regional benchmarks.  For example, recent deals in China appear to be aligned with Anglo’s terms ($60.5/t & 6.05c/lb) while Europe and Japan may be successful in maintaining Freeport’s reference numbers of $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb. Clearly it is still too early to establish (what, in any event, is unlikely to be) a definitive benchmark for 2012, given the sheer number of outstanding deals still to be concluded.  If subsequent settlements in Europe and Japan were to deviate from those fixed thus far, then the concept of a regional benchmark would not be applicable and some mechanism to calculate a representative global average would need to be established.
